content: The kidneys are highly complex organs with multiple essential biological functions. Their primary role is to maintain the homeostatic balance of bodily fluids. This is achieved through the filtration and secretion of metabolites, such as urea, and minerals from the blood, which are then excreted along with water as urine. The kidneys are sensitive to plasma concentrations of compounds like sodium, potassium, hydrogen ions, oxygen, and glucose, making them critical regulators of blood pressure, glucose metabolism, and erythropoiesis. The medical field dedicated to the study of the kidneys and their diseases is known as nephrology. The term nephrooriginates from the Ancient Greek word nephros, meaning kidney, while the adjective renal, meaning related to the kidney, is derived from the Latin word renes. In humans, the kidneys are located in the posterior part of the abdomen, with one on each side of the spine. The right kidney is positioned slightly lower than the left due to the asymmetry caused by the liver. The left kidney is located below the diaphragm and adjacent to the spleen. Each kidney is topped by an adrenal gland (also called the suprarenal gland). The kidneys are retroperitoneal organs, situated approximately at the vertebral levels T12 to L3. The upper parts of the kidneys are partially protected by the 11th and 12th ribs. Each kidney is surrounded by two layers of fat, the perirenal and pararenal fat, which provide cushioning. The kidneys are bean-shaped organs with a concave medial side. On this medial aspect is an opening called the hilum, which allows the entry and exit of the renal artery, renal vein, nerves, and ureter. The outer portion of the kidney is the renal cortex, located just beneath the fibrous capsule. Beneath the cortex lies the renal medulla, which is divided into 10-20 renal pyramids in humans. Each pyramid, along with its overlying cortex, forms a renal lobe. The tip of each pyramid, known as the papilla, empties into a calyx, and the calyces drain into the renal pelvis. The renal pelvis transmits urine to the urinary bladder via the ureter. Humans are typically born with two kidneys but can survive with only one. The upper and lower poles of the kidneys refer to their highest and lowest points. Due to their differing heights, the upper pole of the right kidney aligns with the hilum of the left kidney, which is also at the same level as the transpyloric plane. Each kidney receives its blood supply from the renal artery, which branches from the abdominal aorta. Upon entering the hilum, the renal artery divides into smaller interlobar arteries, which are situated between the renal pyramids. These arteries branch into arcuate arteries at the outer medulla, which run along the border between the medulla and cortex. The arcuate arteries give rise to cortical radial arteries (also called interlobular arteries), which further branch into afferent arterioles supplying the glomerular capillaries. Blood from the glomeruli drains into efferent arterioles, which then form peritubular capillaries that supply the cortex. Blood from these capillaries collects in renal venules and exits the kidney via the renal vein. Efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons send branches into the medulla, forming the vasa recta. Blood supply is closely linked to blood pressure regulation. The kidneys are innervated by the renal and ureteric nerves, which arise from the renal plexus. This innervation includes sympathetic, parasympathetic, and visceral afferent fibers. The renal plexus itself is innervated by thoracic splanchnic nerves, particularly the caudal ones. The nephron is the basic functional unit of the kidney, with over a million nephrons present in the cortex and medulla of each normal adult kidney. Nephrons regulate water and solute balance by filtering blood under pressure, reabsorbing necessary fluids and molecules, and secreting unneeded substances. These processes are facilitated by cotransport and countertransport mechanisms within the nephrons and associated collecting ducts. The collecting duct system is crucial for water conservation. In the presence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also known as vasopressin), these ducts become permeable to water, allowing its reabsorption and concentrating the urine. When excess water needs to be excreted, ADH production decreases, rendering the collecting ducts less permeable to water, resulting in dilute and abundant urine. Failure to appropriately decrease ADH production, as seen in the syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH), can lead to water retention and dangerous dilution of body fluids, potentially causing severe neurological damage. Conversely, failure to produce ADH or the inability of the collecting ducts to respond to it can result in excessive urination, a condition known as diabetes insipidus (DI). The collecting duct system also plays a significant role in maintaining acid-base homeostasis. The kidneys excrete various waste products of metabolism, including nitrogenous wastes like urea (from protein catabolism) and uric acid (from nucleic acid metabolism), as well as water. They are vital for whole-body homeostasis, including acid-base balance, regulation of electrolyte concentrations, control of blood volume, and regulation of blood pressure. These functions are achieved independently and in coordination with other organs, particularly those of the endocrine system, through hormones secreted into the bloodstream. The kidneys regulate pH by eliminating hydrogen ions and maintaining the mineral ion and water composition of the blood. Urine pH can range from acidic (pH 5) to alkaline (pH 8). This regulation involves four main protein transporters: NHE3 (a sodium-hydrogen exchanger), V-type H-ATPase (a hydrogen ATPase isoform), NBC1 (a sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter), and AE1 (an anion exchanger that exchanges chloride for bicarbonate). The polar alignment of renal epithelial cells ensures that NHE3 and H-ATPase are exposed to the lumen on the apical side, facilitating hydrogen ion excretion, while NBC1 and AE1 on the basolateral side allow bicarbonate ions to return to the blood plasma. Sodium ions are regulated through a homeostatic process involving aldosterone, which increases sodium ion reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubules. When blood pressure is low, renin, a proteolytic enzyme, is secreted by the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Renin converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is then converted by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the lung capillaries to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex, which increases sodium reabsorption in the renal tubules, leading to increased water reabsorption, blood volume, and ultimately blood pressure. The kidneys also play a role in regulating plasma osmolality. Any significant change in plasma osmolality is detected by the hypothalamus, which communicates with the posterior pituitary gland. A rise in osmolality triggers the secretion of ADH, promoting water reabsorption by the kidneys and increasing urine concentration. These mechanisms work together to restore plasma osmolality to normal levels. The kidneys secrete various hormones, including erythropoietin, urodilatin, renin, and vitamin D. Kidney development, or nephrogenesis, occurs in three successive phases: the pronephros, mesonephros, and metanephros. The pronephros, appearing around day 22 of human gestation, is nonfunctional in mammals. The mesonephros, which develops next, is similar to the kidneys of aquatic amphibians and fish. The definitive kidney, the metanephros, begins to develop during the fifth week of gestation. The ureteric bud, an outpouching of the mesonephric duct, induces the differentiation of the metanephrogenic blastema into renal tubules, which connect with the collecting duct system to form a continuous passage for urine flow. The kidneys are susceptible to various congenital and acquired diseases. Congenital conditions include hydronephrosis, urinary tract obstruction, duplicated ureters, horseshoe kidney, polycystic kidney disease, renal dysplasia, and multicystic dysplastic kidney. Acquired conditions include diabetic nephropathy, glomerulonephritis, hydronephrosis, interstitial nephritis, kidney stones, renal tumors (e.g., Wilms tumor, renal cell carcinoma), lupus nephritis, minimal change disease, pyelonephritis, and renal failure (acute or chronic). Humans can live with one kidney, as it provides sufficient renal function for survival. However, chronic renal failure develops when the amount of functioning kidney tissue is significantly reduced. End-stage renal failure or severe symptoms of renal dysfunction necessitate renal replacement therapy, such as dialysis or kidney transplantation. Medical terms related to the kidneys often use the prefixes renaland nephro-. Surgical removal of a kidney is called nephrectomy, while a radical nephrectomy involves removing the kidney, surrounding tissue, lymph nodes, and potentially the adrenal gland, often for cancer treatment. World Kidney Day is observed annually on the second Thursday of March to raise awareness of kidney disease and promote prevention and early detection. It is a joint initiative by the International Society of Nephrology (ISN) and the International Federation of Kidney Foundations (IFKF).
